expansion:
15 degree left esotropia is the bank's printed key. The lecture's own worked photograph of the corneal light reflex test supports a temporally-displaced reflex meaning the eye is turned inward, not outward: on the cover-test slide, the fixing eye has its reflex centred, while the deviating eye is described as "TURNED IN toward the nose: its iris is displaced nasally, a wide white crescent of sclera is exposed on its TEMPORAL side, and its corneal light reflex is displaced OUTWARD, sitting toward the temporal edge of the pupil rather than centrally... a manifest convergent deviation — ESOTROPIA" (L29, slide 11). The stem describes exactly this pattern for the left eye — reflex in the temporal part of the pupil, with the right eye's reflex central — so by the lecture's own example this is a left esotropia, matching the printed key of A. The lecture also states plainly that the millimetre-to-degree conversion used to size a deviation from reflex displacement is never printed anywhere in this deck (L29, note on slides 5/11/18), so the specific figure of 15 degrees for this amount of displacement is not taken from the course material.

15 degree left exotropia, option B, describes the correct magnitude class of deviation but the wrong direction: exotropia requires the deviating eye's reflex to be displaced nasally (toward the inner canthus), which is the mirror image of what the lecture's slide 6 diagram shows for exotropia — "the eye ... is turned OUT ... its iris sits against the outer (temporal) corner and the wide white crescent is on the NASAL side" (L29, slide 6) — not the temporal-reflex pattern given in the stem.

45 degree left esotropia, option C, has the correct direction but an unsupported magnitude; the lecture never gives a millimetre-to-degree conversion scale, so no specific angular value, including 45 degrees, can be derived from the stem's description of reflex position alone (not taken from the course material).

45 degree left exotropia, option D, is wrong on both counts: it inverts the direction (exotropia would need a nasally displaced reflex, not the temporal one described) and assigns an unsupported magnitude for the same reason as option C.

Discrepancy note: the page marks A (15 degree left esotropia) as the key, but its own printed explanation box reasons toward exotropia, stating "A temporal light reflex means the eye is deviated outward (exotropia)". This directly contradicts the lecture's own worked example, in which a temporally displaced corneal light reflex is used to demonstrate esotropia, not exotropia. Per standing rule, the printed key (A) is not disputed or moved; the box's stated reasoning is recorded here as a discrepancy only, without a ruling on which physiological direction convention the box's authors intended.
objective: Interpret a temporally displaced corneal light reflex on Hirschberg-style testing as esotropia, matching the lecture's own worked example
